title: Quiz: Individuals and Moving Range (I-MR) Charts

questions.text: Given x̄ = 200ms, MR̄ = 15ms, and d₂ = 1.128, what is the UCL of the Individuals chart?
Why is the standard deviation estimated as MR̄/d₂ (where d₂ = 1.128) rather than computing the sample standard deviation directly from all observations?
options: MR̄/d₂ estimates short-term variation between consecutive observations, excluding the effect of process shifts
The sample standard deviation is always larger than the true σ for small samples
d₂ = 1.128 is a correction for skewed data
MR̄/d₂ is less sensitive to outliers than the sample standard deviation
questions.explanation: MR̄/d₂ captures only the short-term, consecutive-observation variation — the natural process noise. If a process shift has occurred, the overall sample standard deviation would be inflated, making the limits too wide to detect the shift.

questions.text: An ETL job runs once daily. Runtimes are measured each day. Which control chart should you use?
options: I-MR chart — one measurement per day, no natural subgrouping
Xbar-R chart — use daily means of hourly sub-runs
c chart — runtimes are counts of events
questions.explanation: With one measurement per day and no natural subgrouping, the I-MR chart is correct. Xbar-R requires multiple measurements per subgroup. p and c charts are for attribute (count/proportion) data, not continuous runtimes.

questions.text: The MR chart signals out of control when:
options: A moving range exceeds UCL_MR = D₄ × MR̄
The cumulative sum of observations exceeds a threshold
More than 2 consecutive moving ranges are above MR̄
questions.explanation: The MR chart signals when any single moving range MRᵢ > UCL_MR = D₄ × MR̄ = 3.267 × MR̄. This indicates an unusually large jump between two consecutive observations — evidence of an abrupt process change.

questions.text: The I-MR chart is as robust to non-normality as the Xbar-R chart.
questions.explanation: The Xbar chart benefits from the Central Limit Theorem — subgroup means are approximately normal even when individual measurements are not. The I chart plots raw individual measurements, so it relies more directly on the normality assumption. Non-normal data can significantly distort the false alarm rate of an I chart.
